title: why the glass breaks
hook: one stomp, a crunch, and everyone shouts mazel tov: why break something at a wedding?

segments.voice: Yesterday: the seder, a story laid out as food. Your line was we were slaves. Today, the loudest second of a Jewish wedding.

The end of the ceremony. The couple stands under a canopy. Someone sets a glass, wrapped in a cloth, on the floor. One stomp, a crunch, and the whole room shouts mazel tov. Plenty of people have cheered for it without knowing why it happens. And there's more than one answer: families tell it different ways.
screen: `A GLASS IN A CLOTH.` → `ONE STOMP.` → `MAZEL TOV!`

segments.voice: Start with the canopy. It's called a chuppah: four poles and a cloth, open on every side, like the roof of a home that's just beginning. Then the glass. Its roots go back to rabbis in ancient Babylon who broke a precious cup at a wedding feast, on purpose, when the celebrating got out of hand. Later teachers tied the custom to Jerusalem, and the Temple that stood there, destroyed nearly two thousand years ago. An old psalm promises to keep Jerusalem above even your highest joy. So at the happiest moment, something breaks: a reminder that even on the best day, something in the world is still broken. Families add their own readings. Love is precious and breakable, so handle it with care. A glass, once broken, stays broken; the promise is meant to be just as permanent. In some old customs, the noise scared off bad luck. Traditionally the groom breaks it; at many weddings today, either partner does, or both together. More than one meaning can be true at once, and a Jewish wedding is happy to hold them all. Then comes the shout, the words you met two days ago: mazel tov.
screen: `THE CHUPPAH — OPEN ON EVERY SIDE.` · `A PRECIOUS CUP, BROKEN.` · `REMEMBER JERUSALEM.` · `MORE THAN ONE MEANING.`

segments.voice: Three breaths with the bell. First breath: the happiest moment you can remember. Second breath: someone or something missing from it. Third breath: let the two sit side by side, without either one canceling the other.
The glass. Broken at the height of the joy, so the joy remembers. Fifth word.
Your line: even in joy, remember. The crunch comes right before the cheering, never instead of it. That's day five.

original.note: Hebrew: the breaking of the glass (kos, a cup or glass).

trapdoor: what you thought: a fun wedding stunt.
what it means: breaking something at the height of joy, so the joy remembers what's still broken.

what a scholar hears: Berakhot 30b–31a has rabbis breaking costly cups to sober a wedding feast; later custom links it to remembering Jerusalem and Psalm 137:6, setting Jerusalem above one's chief joy.

story.title: the cup worth a fortune
story.text: A rabbi is throwing a wedding feast for his son, and the most learned guests in town are getting very, very merry. He walks out with the most expensive cup in the house, worth a small fortune, and smashes it on the floor in front of them. The room goes quiet. At another wedding, another rabbi does the same with a cup of fine white glass. The rabbis who tell the story aren't against joy; they just want it with one eye open.

wrong.myth: breaking the glass has one official meaning.
wrong.truth: families tell it several ways: remembering Jerusalem, love's fragility, a promise that can't be undone. more than one can be true.

sources.ref: Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 30b–31a (Mar son of Ravina and Rav Ashi break costly cups at wedding feasts)
Tosafot to Berakhot 31a (the custom of breaking a glass at weddings); Shulchan Aruch, Orach Chaim 560:2, with the Rema (remembering Jerusalem at a wedding)
Family explanations of the custom (fragility of love, an irreversible promise, warding off bad luck), as collected in the audience research (18Doors; Modern Tribe; Chabad.org)

notes: New lesson 2026-10-06 (research: 'breaking the glass: several stories, one moment'); deliberately teaches 'more than one meaning can be true'.

Jerusalem and the Temple are mentioned only as the historical memory the custom keeps (the Second Temple's destruction, 70 CE, given as 'nearly two thousand years ago'); nothing about the modern city or politics. Confirm the framing.
Berakhot 30b–31a: Mar son of Ravina broke a cup worth 400 zuz; Rav Ashi a cup of white glass. Told without names and numbers. Confirm.
The link between the glass and remembering Jerusalem is a later explanation (Tosafot; Rema to Orach Chaim 560:2 on remembering Jerusalem at weddings; Kol Bo). Confirm the citations.
'Traditionally the groom; at many weddings today, either partner or both': confirm wording across movements and for same-sex weddings.
The folk reading (noise scaring off bad luck or spirits) is given as 'some old customs', per the research's 'be honest when an explanation is folklore'.
